bib.title: Harness Engineering for Software Engineering via Modular Executable Dev-Primitives

legacy_report:
COVERAGE: 30 pages, 102,615 chars. I read the main text (pp. 1-10) and Appendix A and E-G and I. I did not read Appendix B-D (component specs, prompt templates, algorithm, pp. ~14-21) or the Appendix H Qwen3-8B trajectory (pp. ~28-29) line by line. Skipped: references. Extraction was clean. There were no embedded instructions.

SOURCE: "Harness Engineering for Software Engineering via Modular Executable Dev-Primitives" (HERMES). Haibo Jin, Xinjie Li, Peng Kuang, Haohan Wang (corresponding). UIUC, with Penn State for Li. Preprint, arXiv 2610.07832v1 [cs.SE], 6 Oct 2026. The paper does not say it is peer reviewed.

CORE CLAIM: Each repository file (source, config or test) is wrapped with its own resident LLM, called a "Dev-Primitive". Primitives are activated on demand along dependency edges, message only the components they affect, and are revised through a diagnosis step that maps test failures back to the owning component. The paper says this beats matched baseline harnesses.

MECHANISM
- Activation: one LLM call chain localizes components and expands to callers, callees, configs and tests (not a precomputed call graph).
- Collaboration: each primitive reads its own artifact plus the messages sent to it, then edits its artifact and sends messages to the components it implicates.
- Execution: the repository is run and tested.
- Diagnosis: one LLM call returns PASS or FAIL plus (failure, root cause with implicated components, guidance). Only the implicated primitives are reactivated, up to a budget of B=3 rounds.

HEADLINE NUMBERS
- Average gain is +12.4 pp over matched baseline harnesses. Setup: default GPT-5.6 Sol, medium effort, 4 benchmarks, HERMES run once per backbone. Only the harness differs between the paired rows.
- SWE-bench Verified (n=500): 97.0 vs 96.2 (mini-SWE-agent) for GPT-5.6 Sol. Gains are up to +19.4 (GPT-5 Mini); Claude Opus 5 ties. Cost per task is usually higher, e.g. $1.80 vs $1.15.
- SWE Refactor Bench (20 tasks): GPT-5.6 Sol medium goes from 6.5 to 31.0 (+24.5) against Codex. Cost goes from $6.0 to $24.8. Three repeats gave 29.5, 32.0 and 31.5, i.e. 31.0±1.3.
- Terminal-Bench 4.0 (66 tasks, 5 runs each): GPT-5.6 Sol medium goes from 33.0 to 51.8, with tokens rising from 3.6B to 6.8B and cost from $1.9k to $3.4k. Claude Opus 5 gains only +1.5. Claude Sonnet 5 gains +25.2 while using fewer tokens and costing less.
- DevOps-Gym: GPT-5.6 Sol average goes from 49.89 (Codex) to 55.41. Single run, no variance reported.
- Heterogeneous setup: GPT-5.6 Sol activation, Qwen3-8B primitives and GPT-5.5 diagnosis reach 49.7% on Terminal-Bench, against 51.8% for homogeneous Sol. Cost is $2.13k vs $3.40k (-37.4%).
  - The abstract's "-26.2%" and "within 4.5 pp" figures are not directly reproduced in the tables I read.
  - Strong diagnosis helps more than strong activation: on Terminal-Bench, +18.5 vs +9.1 over all-Qwen3-8B.
- Selection quality (GPT-5.6 Sol): recall 83-95%, precision 65-73%, 4.7-12.6 primitives activated per task.

ABLATIONS (GPT-5.6 Sol, drop in points on SWE-bench / Refactor / Terminal / DevOps)
- No inter-primitive communication: -2.8 / -7.5 / -5.7 / -5.07
- No on-demand activation: -1.2 / -3.0 / -2.4 / -2.15. Cost rises 1.61-1.88x, and primitive calls rise from 9.6-25.1 to 28.7-64.3.
- No execution feedback: -3.2 / -9.5 / -8.2 / -7.24
- No diagnosis feedback: -4.4 / -11.0 / -10.6 / -8.68
- Single central editor over the same selected files: 93.4 / 16.8 / 38.8 / 44.21, using 10-14% fewer tokens.
  - A compute-matched editor on Terminal-Bench reaches 45.5 vs 51.8 for HERMES at about the same tokens (6.7B vs 6.8B).
- Revision budget: B=0 to 3 adds 4.8 to 12.5 points; B=3 to 5 adds at most 0.9.
- The same ordering holds for Claude Sonnet 5 and Qwen3-8B (Table 11).

QUOTES
- p.9: "Replacing Dev-Primitives with a centralized editor over the same selected components is the most damaging, 14.2 points on SWE Refactor Bench and 13.0 on Terminal-Bench, and a compute-matched editor still trails HERMES by 6.3 points"
- p.4: "Cross-file changes are coordinated this way without any single context holding every modified component at once."
- p.4: "Messages are directed rather than broadcast."
- p.29 (Limitations): "HERMES introduces additional inference cost and latency because it invokes multiple Dev-Primitives, executes the repository, and performs iterative diagnosis."

LIMITS (authors' own, plus what I see)
- Authors concede: extra cost and latency; small gains where models are saturated; dependence on correct activation and on informative execution feedback; file-level granularity only; only 4 benchmarks; Qwen3-8B was served locally on Ollama with a 32K context.
- Baseline numbers are a mix of leaderboard-reported results and the authors' own matched runs (F.8). HERMES is run once per backbone; only Terminal-Bench (5 runs) and one Refactor repeat report variance.
- SWE Refactor Bench has only 20 tasks.
- Several backbones are model names I cannot verify (GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Fable 5). Treat them as the paper's claims.
- Not shown: any evaluation of subagent context isolation as such, handoff formats, a comparison of topologies, or multi-agent failure modes such as message loss or cascading error.
- It does not compare against other multi-agent topologies beyond a single editor and a Table 5 reference to MAGIS and CodeTeam on different settings.

BUILDS ON: SWE-agent (Yang et al., 2024), OpenHands (Wang et al., 2025), CodeAct (Wang et al., 2024), Agentless (Xia et al., 2025), AutoCodeRover (Zhang et al., 2024). Role-based multi-agent work: MAGIS (Tao et al., NeurIPS 2024), CodeTeam (Wang et al., 2026b), CodeR (Chen et al., 2024), MarsCode (Liu et al., 2024). The authors' own Agent Primitives (Jin et al., 2026a, arXiv 2602.03695) and Tool Primitives (Jin et al., 2026b, arXiv 2609.01736). Context management: Context as a Tool (Liu et al., ACL Findings 2026).

FIT: The note 07-orchestration fits partially. The strongest evidence is the "central editor vs per-component workers" ablation and directed messaging along dependency edges. It also gives a numeric "when multi-agent pays" signal: the gain is larger on cross-file tasks and small on SWE-bench. Cost is higher in most configurations. The paper also supports 08 maturity (cost-versus-model tradeoff, small workers with a strong planner and diagnoser) and 05 verification (diagnosis feedback is the largest ablation, and execution feedback is next). Any of these notes could use it. It is not a general multi-agent paper: it is a software-engineering-specific, single-group preprint.

FIGURE CANDIDATE: Figure 1 (p.3), the HERMES overview: activation, collaboration, execution, diagnosis, loop. It shows the topology and the diagnosis routing at a glance. The extracted text is garbled, so check it visually.
